strengths: The manuscript presents a useful and technically coherent framework for unifying many VRP variants through attribute composition, a shared environment, and a neural policy that can handle node/global attributes. The formulation is clear enough to understand how capacity, open routes, duration limits, time windows, backhauls, mixed backhauls, and multi-depots are represented and masked during decoding.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the neural VRP literature: 16 main variants at 50 and 100 nodes, additional OOD attribute tests, CVRPLIB transfer, and finetuning experiments over mixed-backhaul and multi-depot variants. ROUTEFINDER consistently improves over recent neural multi-task baselines such as MTPOMO and MVMoE, and the finetuning results for EAL are especially convincing relative to standard adapter layers.

The paper includes useful ablations of the transformer encoder changes, global attribute embeddings, mixed batch training, and reward normalization. The mixed-batch and reward-normalization ideas are simple but well motivated for multi-variant RL training, and the ablations support their practical value.

Presentation is generally strong. The paper is well organized, figures communicate the overall architecture and attributes clearly, and the appendix gives many implementation details, hyperparameters, data-generation rules, environment logic, licenses, and additional tables.

The limitations discussion is reasonably honest: the authors acknowledge that neural solution quality remains below strong OR solvers and that the current model is specialized to VRPs rather than a broader CO foundation model. No major unresolved ethical issue is apparent for this type of work.
weaknesses: The main originality is moderate. Several ingredients are adaptations or combinations of established components: POMO-style autoregressive RL, standard transformer modernization, attribute composition from prior multi-task VRP work, simple per-task reward normalization, and zero-initialized feature expansion for adapters. The contribution is useful engineering and synthesis, but not a major conceptual breakthrough.

The “foundation model” framing is somewhat overstated. The model is trained on synthetic distributions for a fixed family of hand-specified VRP attributes and still requires explicit environment/mask engineering for each constraint. Generalization to genuinely new business constraints is only demonstrated for two structured attributes with added input dimensions and finetuning, not for broader unseen VRP formulations.

Although ROUTEFINDER beats neural baselines, it often remains substantially worse than HGS/PyVRP and sometimes OR-Tools in solution quality, especially in unseen multi-depot/mixed-backhaul settings where zero-shot gaps exceed 40% and even EAL remains around 7-19% from HGS. This limits the practical significance unless very fast inference is the dominant requirement.

Some comparisons are not fully satisfying. The baselines are mostly constructive neural solvers; the paper does not compare against stronger neural improvement/search methods under matched wall-clock budgets, nor does it deeply analyze quality-time tradeoffs beyond reporting that neural methods are faster. Claims about real-world usefulness would be stronger with anytime curves or hybrid local-search experiments.

Reproducibility is decent but not complete from the manuscript alone. Many hyperparameters and generation rules are included, and the authors state code is public, but the exact code URL/footnote was not visible in the extracted manuscript, and the large training cost plus on-the-fly synthetic generation make independent reproduction nontrivial. Statistical uncertainty across seeds is also not reported.

Some empirical interpretations rely on weak evidence. The t-SNE cluster visualizations are presented as indicators of better representation and generalization, but they are qualitative and not decisive. Several ablation plots show small average-gap differences, and the paper does not report variance or significance tests to separate robust gains from run-to-run noise.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant direction: reusable neural solvers for families of vehicle routing problems rather than one-off models for individual variants.

The unified attribute-based VRP environment is a useful engineering contribution, and the paper gives reasonably detailed descriptions of the supported attributes, data generation, action masking, and hyperparameters.

The empirical section is broad relative to many NCO papers: it compares against recent multi-task neural baselines, includes ablations, studies out-of-distribution attribute values, evaluates CVRPLIB large instances, and considers fine-tuning to unseen attributes.

The proposed Efficient Adapter Layers have a clear rationale: zero-initializing new feature dimensions preserves the pretrained model at step 0, and the fine-tuning results consistently improve over the adapter-layer baseline.
weaknesses: The central 'foundation model' framing is overstated. The model is trained and evaluated mostly on synthetic uniform VRP distributions with a fixed family of handcrafted attributes, and the strongest results are incremental improvements over closely related multi-task VRP solvers rather than evidence of broad foundation-model behavior.

The main in-distribution evaluation is less convincing than advertised. Table 1 covers 16 variants at 50 and 100 nodes, while the paper repeatedly emphasizes 48 variants; many of the additional variants appear only in zero-shot/fine-tuning studies. This makes the '48 variants' claim feel inflated.

The method remains far from competitive with traditional solvers in solution quality. HGS/PyVRP defines the best-known solution in most tables, while ROUTE FINDER often has gaps of 1-5% on synthetic 50/100-node cases and much larger gaps in unseen MD/MB settings. The paper emphasizes speed, but the comparison uses very different compute regimes and does not present a fair quality-time tradeoff curve.

Several claimed components are individually weak or under-justified. The transformer encoder changes are mostly standard modern Transformer substitutions, reward normalization appears to have a very small effect in Appendix D.4, and Mixed Batch Training is intuitive but not deeply analyzed beyond training curves.

The fine-tuning story is only partially convincing. EAL improves over AL and scratch training under a small 10-epoch budget, but absolute gaps for harder unseen variants remain large, e.g. roughly 7-19% in the combined multi-depot mixed-backhaul setting, and often worse than OR-Tools. This limits the practical significance of the adaptation claim.

Reproducibility is not adequate as written. The manuscript says the code is publicly available and later invites readers to inspect source code, but the extracted PDF shows missing/blank links. The paper gives many implementation details, but without an accessible repository the unified environment and baseline retraining choices are hard to verify.

The experimental reporting lacks uncertainty estimates, statistical tests, and enough clarity about whether baseline models were retrained under identical data distributions and compute budgets. Given that many improvements over MVMoE/MTPOMO are modest, variance matters.

The ethics/impact statement is perfunctory. For routing optimization, deployment can affect labor conditions, emissions, service equity, and surveillance/logistics decisions; saying there are no consequences to highlight is not an adequate treatment of downstream impacts.

Presentation is generally readable, but some claims are too sweeping relative to the evidence, and some tables are dense enough that the main empirical message is hard to audit. The paper would benefit from clearer separation between engineering contribution, algorithmic novelty, and empirical gains.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and practically relevant problem: building a unified neural solver for many VRP variants rather than training separate models per variant. The unified MDOVRPMBLTW environment and attribute-composition formulation are useful infrastructure contributions for the NCO/VRP community.

The empirical evaluation is broad by current standards. The main experiments cover 16 in-distribution variants at 50 and 100 nodes, with additional appendices expanding to 48 variants including mixed backhaul and multi-depot settings, OOD attribute values, and large CVRPLIB instances.

The proposed components are well motivated and mostly well supported: global attribute embeddings, mixed batch training, reward normalization, a modernized transformer encoder, and efficient adapter layers each receive targeted ablations or supplementary experiments.

The fine-tuning results with Efficient Adapter Layers are particularly compelling. EAL preserves zero-shot behavior by construction and consistently improves over standard adapter layers, scratch training, and single-variant fine-tuning baselines on unseen MB/MD attributes.

Reproducibility is relatively strong: the manuscript gives detailed generation procedures, environment logic, model architecture, hyperparameters, hardware, licenses, and claims public code availability. The appendices are unusually detailed for implementation-relevant aspects.
weaknesses: The novelty of several modeling components is somewhat incremental: RMSNorm/pre-norm/SwiGLU/FlashAttention are imported from modern transformer practice, while reward normalization and adapter zero-initialization are natural extensions. The main originality is in system integration and empirical demonstration rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The “foundation model” framing is somewhat stronger than the evidence warrants. The model generalizes across a designed family of synthetic VRP attributes, but it remains specialized to Euclidean, randomly generated VRP distributions and does not yet demonstrate broad transfer across substantially different real logistics regimes or problem classes.

Traditional solvers such as HGS-PyVRP remain much better in solution quality in many tables, with the neural model’s advantage mainly being inference time. This is a valid tradeoff, but the paper sometimes emphasizes state-of-the-art performance without sufficiently foregrounding that the claim is primarily relative to neural baselines.

The evaluation lacks statistical uncertainty over training seeds or confidence intervals. Given that many in-distribution improvements over MVMoE/MTPOMO are modest in absolute gap, seed variability could matter for some component-level claims.

The public-code footnote appears incomplete or not visible in the extracted manuscript, and the paper would benefit from clearer artifact details such as exact repository URL, checkpoints, data-generation scripts, and evaluation commands.

The impact statement is cursory. While the work has no obvious major ethical issue, VRP solvers can affect labor allocation, delivery routing, emissions, and operational decisions; a short discussion of these deployment considerations would be more appropriate.
